title: Understand These American Phrases? You're Advanced | For Intermediate And Advanced English Learners
channel: Speak English with Bo's Slow English

lines.text: Hello everyone. Welcome to a new episode
of Bo's Slow English. If you are an
intermediate English learner on your way
to advanced, this lesson is perfect for
you because I will be speaking at more
of a moderate pace and I will teach you
cultural fluency, which means that not
only do you understand the words, but
you also understand the meaning behind
it. If you are a beginner English
learner, this video may also be
interesting for you because it will give
you an introduction
to where you will want to go hopefully
in several months. If we've never met
before, my name is Bo. It is nice to
meet you. I usually create slow speaking
vlog style videos, but as I mentioned,
today is going to be a moderate speaking
style. This video was requested by one
of my subscribers. So, thank you for
your suggestion. So, I know that I
mentioned that we will be talking about
cultural fluency and this is going to be
specifically in regards to what
Americans mean. Today, I'll explain a
few common American phrases that confuse
English learners and what the meaning is
behind these phrases. Before we get
started, please hit the like button to
show your support. It keeps me motivated
to continue making these videos. And
also, if we aren't friends yet, please
click the subscribe button so that we
can get to know each other. Number one,
have you ever heard an American say, "We
should hang out sometime." The literal
meaning for this is we want to meet. The
real meaning is friendly,
but it doesn't actually mean that
someone wants to meet. In other words,
there are no actual plans to meet. So,
if someone says this to you, but they
don't suggest a time or place, they're
just saying it to be nice. Number two,
"How are you?" Even though this is a
question,
it's not an actual question for you to
answer in depths. The polite answer and
the typical answer is, "I'm good,
thanks. How about you?" Let's say you're
having a bad day,
you
shouldn't say that you're having a bad
day. Unless you know the person, that's
fine. It's not the time or the place to
have an emotional check-in. So, don't
say,
"Uh, I'm having a really bad day. I
don't know. I feel like I feel like the
world is coming to an end." It's not a
conversation like that. Just say, "I'm
good. And you?" Number three,
if someone says, "Maybe, let's see.
Let me get back to you."
It's a polite way of saying probably
not. These terms are used to
not directly say no because if you flat
out say no, you might offend someone.
Culturally, Americans try to avoid
sounding too negative. So, that is why
they would say, "Maybe.
Let's see.
Let me get back to you." Number four,
"That's interesting."
This phrase can be said in multiple
tones just like the other phrases that I
mentioned, but generally, if someone's
saying, "That's interesting," they're
not actually interested, they're curious
or they don't agree or they're confused.
It's really important to listen to the
tone. Is it awkward? Is it genuine? In
the beginning of learning English, it
may be difficult for you to pick up on
the different facial expressions and the
tones, but just be careful when you do
hear and interpret someone saying,
"That's interesting," because it may be
slightly negative. Number five, "I'm
good, thanks." Some people may use this
phrase in response to an offer. What
this phrase means is, "No, thank you."
It doesn't mean that they're actually
good, which I can totally understand how
this is confusing, but it's just
something that Americans say. "I'm good,
thanks." For example, my mom wanted to
give me another bowl of rice and I would
say, "I'm good, thanks."
And that is my way of saying, "No, thank
you." To summarize, these phrases are
often used by Americans and if you are
an intermediate to advanced learner, it
is important for you to understand the
meaning behind these phrases, but it'll
be easier for you to understand if you
watch the body language and you listen
to the tone and you keep in mind the
overall context of the conversation. I
know American English can be very
difficult. I'm here to help make your
journey easier. So, I hope that this
lesson was helpful. Let me know in the
comments, in your country, what phrases
are used that have a completely
different meaning. I would love to know.
Don't forget to like and subscribe and I
will see you next time. Bye.
